title.en: Molecules, covalent bonds and ionic bonds

text.en: Think of friends sharing a notebook so that both can study, and of a shopkeeper giving a coin to a customer in a fair exchange. Atoms do something like this too. Some share electrons, some hand them over, and in both cases they end up more stable than before.

A molecule is an electrically neutral group of more than one atom that can exist on its own and shows all the properties of that substance. A hydrogen molecule has two hydrogen atoms, and a hydrogen chloride molecule has one hydrogen and one chlorine atom.
Some elements, such as helium, exist only as single atoms because their atoms are already stable.
An atom is stable with 8 electrons in its valence shell, or 2 if the K shell is the outermost. Atoms with fewer electrons share, gain or lose electrons to reach this.
When atoms combine, the energy of the system falls below the total energy of the separate atoms, so the arrangement is more stable. The force that holds the atoms together is a chemical bond.
In a covalent bond atoms share electrons. Hydrogen has one electron and needs one more to fill its K shell, so two hydrogen atoms share one pair and form H2, written H-H, a single bond.
Chlorine has seven valence electrons and needs one more, so two chlorine atoms share one pair to make Cl2, written Cl-Cl.
Oxygen has six valence electrons and needs two, so two oxygen atoms share two pairs of electrons. They are joined by a double bond, written O=O.
Atoms of different elements also share. In hydrogen chloride one hydrogen and one chlorine share a pair, H-Cl. In water, oxygen needs two electrons, so it shares one with each of two hydrogen atoms, giving H2O.
Covalent compounds are named using prefixes: mono, di, tri, tetra, penta, hexa. CO is carbon monoxide, CO2 is carbon dioxide, SF6 is sulfur hexafluoride, and N2O5 is dinitrogen pentoxide. The first element gets no mono, and hydrogen as first element gets no prefix, so H2S is hydrogen sulfide.
In an ionic bond, electrons are transferred. A sodium atom (11 protons) loses its one valence electron and becomes a sodium cation, Na+, with 11 protons and 10 electrons.
A chlorine atom gains that electron and becomes a chloride anion, Cl-. The opposite charges attract strongly, and this electrostatic attraction between ions is the ionic bond in sodium chloride.
In a crystal of sodium chloride each Na+ is surrounded by six Cl- and each Cl- by six Na+, in a repeating three-dimensional pattern called a crystal lattice. So ionic compounds form crystals, not separate molecules.
Metals usually form cations and non-metals form anions. Sulfur gains two electrons to become S2-, and magnesium loses two to become Mg2+. Ionic compounds are named cation first, then the anion with the ending -ide, for example sodium chloride and calcium oxide.
Ions with more than one kind of atom, such as OH-, NO3-, CO3 2-, SO4 2- and NH4+, are polyatomic ions. Their names do not usually end in -ide.

problem.en: Show how magnesium chloride is formed from magnesium (2, 8, 2) and chlorine (2, 8, 7).

text.en: Magnesium has 2 valence electrons. Losing both gives the stable arrangement 2, 8, so it forms Mg2+.

why.en: Metals with fewer than four valence electrons tend to lose them.

text.en: Chlorine has 7 valence electrons and needs only 1 more to reach 8, so it forms Cl-.

why.en: Non-metals with more than four valence electrons tend to gain.

text.en: One magnesium atom gives 2 electrons, but each chlorine atom accepts only 1, so two chlorine atoms are needed.

why.en: The electrons given must equal the electrons taken.

text.en: One Mg2+ ion and two Cl- ions are held together by electrostatic attraction. This is an ionic bond and the compound is magnesium chloride, MgCl2.

prompt.en: Compare how a covalent bond and an ionic bond form, using one example of each.

requiredIdeas.en: Covalent bond: atoms share electrons, for example hydrogen chloride H-Cl
Ionic bond: one atom transfers electrons to another to form oppositely charged ions that attract, for example sodium chloride
Both help atoms reach a stable octet or duplet

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking ionic compounds form separate molecules
Thinking the shared electrons in a covalent bond belong to only one atom

points.en: A molecule is a neutral group of atoms that can exist independently and shows the properties of the substance.
A covalent bond forms by sharing electrons; an ionic bond forms by transfer of electrons and the attraction between ions.
Metals tend to form cations and non-metals anions; ionic compounds form crystals, not molecules.
Covalent compounds are named with prefixes; ionic compounds with cation first and anion ending in -ide.
